# Voice — replacing the browser's speech with recorded lines

The game speaks everything it shows (hard rule #5). Until now that has been
`SpeechSynthesis`, and for release it is not good enough: the voice is different
on every browser and platform, several of them are unpleasant, none of them
sound like they are talking to a three-year-old, and the ones that mispronounce
a place name mispronounce it confidently.

**The decision: pre-recorded lines, generated by an offline TTS engine, shipped
with the game.** This file is the plan. It lives outside `SCENE_GUIDE.md` and
`SCENE_ROADMAP.md` on purpose — those come from the scene collaborator and are
overwritten by every art drop.

---

## It is smaller than it feels

Everything the game says comes from `play/js/i18n.js` or `play/js/world.js`.
Counted:

| | lines |
|---|---|
| place names, English | 37 |
| place names, Polish | 10 — the other 27 have no Polish form and are *deliberately* spoken in English (decision #6) |
| state names | 51, English only — they are American proper nouns |
| UI strings | ~68 English, ~70 Polish |
| **total** | **~218** |

At mono MP3 that is roughly **1.5 MB of audio, 2 MB inlined as base64** — under
half of what `asset-data.js` already ships. Size is not the constraint.

Phase 2 adds numbers, letters, shapes and praise words. Record them in the same
session with the same voice, or you will be doing this twice.

---

## Where it plugs in

Hard rule #5 has been earning its keep: **nothing outside `play/js/speech.js`
calls `SpeechSynthesis`**. This is a change inside one module, not a sweep.

### Key the clips by the string, not by an id

The obvious design is `speech.line('place.chicago')`, which means threading a key
through every call site. Don't. Every spoken string already comes from a
dictionary, so **the text is the key** — slug it and look it up.

That buys three things:

- **No call-site changes.** `speech.say(text, { lang })` keeps its signature.
- **A generator that cannot invent work.** It walks `i18n.js` and `world.js` and
  emits exactly the lines that exist.
- **A checker.** `tools/check-voice.py` reports strings with no clip and clips
  with no string. Edit a string and the audio goes stale — that has to be a
  build error, not something a child discovers. Same discipline as
  `check-scenes.py`, and the "four places must agree" list becomes five.

### One sprite per language, played through `audio.js`

Not 218 files. Concatenate each language into a single MP3 plus a
`{ slug: [startSeconds, durationSeconds] }` index, generated into
`play/js/voice-en.js` and `play/js/voice-pl.js` the same way `asset-data.js`
inlines the scenes. `file://` keeps working and there is still no build step
required to *run* the game.

Play it through the **Web Audio context that `audio.js` already owns**, not an
`<audio>` element. That reuses:

- the gesture unlock already wired to **ALL ABOARD**,
- the existing mute setting,
- and `start(when, offset, duration)`, which plays a slice cleanly and cancels
  precisely — which `<audio>` seeking does not.

One number to keep an eye on: decoding a ~110-second sprite holds roughly
**10 MB of PCM per language** at 22 kHz mono. Fine on anything modern. If it
hurts on an old tablet, fall back to individual clips decoded on demand and
cached — more decodes, far less resident memory.

### The robot stays as the safety net

**Clip if we have one, `SpeechSynthesis` if we do not, silence never.** Decision
#5 exists because a child who hears nothing thinks the game is broken, and that
has not changed. It also means the audio can land incrementally: record the 37
place names first and everything else keeps working while you go.

---

## Generating it with Piper

[Piper](https://github.com/rhasspy/piper) is MIT-licensed, runs entirely
offline, and needs no account or API key. Suitable for a free, open-source
project where the generated audio is redistributed.

### Yes, the voice can be varied — three ways

1. **Pick a different voice model.** Each is an `.onnx` + `.onnx.json` pair, and
   there are many per language. English has a lot of choice; **Polish has
   noticeably fewer**, which is the real constraint on this project.
2. **Multi-speaker models.** Some models carry many speakers in one file and take
   `--speaker <id>`, so one download gives a range of voices.
3. **Delivery controls.** `--length_scale` (higher is slower), `--noise_scale`
   and `--noise_w` (how much variation in tone and phoneme length), and
   `--sentence_silence`. Slowing slightly is usually the single biggest
   improvement for this audience.

What Piper does **not** give you is a pitch dial. If a voice needs lifting,
that is a post-process (`ffmpeg`/`rubberband`, formant-preserving) — and go
gently, because a chipmunk narrator is worse than a plain one.

> The voice roster changes; check the current list rather than trusting names
> written down here.

### THE LICENCE TRAP — read this before choosing a voice

**Piper being MIT does not make its voices MIT.** Each voice model carries the
licence of the data it was trained on: some are CC0 or CC-BY, others are not
freely redistributable. This project ships the generated audio inside the
repository, so the voice's licence has to permit that.

Check the licence of the specific voice, record it in this file next to the
voice name, and give attribution if the licence asks for it. This is the same
call that ruled out the Rocky statue in Philadelphia and keeps badges and team
liveries out of Indianapolis and Detroit.

### A warm adult beats a fake child

The instinct is to reach for a child-sounding voice. Resist it. A warm, clear
adult reading slowly is easier for a three-year-old to follow and does not go
uncanny. What actually helps: a slightly slower rate, generous silence at the
end of each line, and consistent volume across clips (normalise them).

### The two languages will not be the same voice

English and Polish come from different models trained on different speakers, so
the narrator inherently changes when the language does. That is unavoidable
short of hiring one bilingual human. Pick two voices that at least share a
register — both warm, both unhurried, similar apparent age — so it reads as a
different narrator rather than a different game.

---

## What we get beyond consistency

Pronunciation. The browser voices currently mangle **Oʻahu**, **Quechee**,
**Ketchum**, **Albuquerque** and **Savannah**, and `world.spoken()` carries a
whole `sayAs` mechanism purely so Washington DC is read as letters rather than
slurred. With recordings those are simply said correctly, and that machinery
becomes decoration rather than load-bearing.

---

## Open, and the maintainer's call

- **One narrator, or a narrator plus a train character?** A second voice for the
  train ("all aboard!") is charming and doubles the recording work.
- **Do the state names need Polish?** Today they are always English, on the
  grounds that they are American proper nouns. Recording changes nothing about
  that decision — it is here only so nobody re-opens it by accident.
- **Sound effects stay where they are.** The bell, whistle, chuff and honk are
  synthesised in `audio.js` and are not part of this. They already sound the
  same everywhere.

---

## Definition of done

- [ ] a voice chosen per language, with its licence recorded above
- [ ] `tools/gen-voice.py` — walks the dictionaries, drives Piper, normalises,
      concatenates, writes `play/js/voice-<lang>.js`
- [ ] `tools/check-voice.py` — strings with no clip, clips with no string
- [ ] `speech.js` prefers a clip, falls back to `SpeechSynthesis`, never silent
- [ ] playback through `audio.js`'s context, honouring the existing mute
- [ ] verified on `file://` **and** served, and on a real iPhone — audio unlock
      and autoplay policy are exactly the sort of thing headless Chrome will
      happily tell you is fine
